articles.title: How to Prepare for the HR Round in a Developer Interview
articles.excerpt: You cleared the coding round, and now there is one more call: the HR round. Many developers treat it as a formality and walk in with no plan. That is a mistake. A strong HR round can decide between tw…
articles.body: You cleared the coding round, and now there is one more call: the HR round. Many developers treat it as a formality and walk in with no plan. That is a mistake. A strong HR round can decide between two candidates with similar technical scores. Here is a simple way to prepare. What the HR round actually checks What they check What it means for you Communication Can you explain your work in plain words? Teamwork Can you work with testers, designers and managers? Attitude Do you handle feedback and pressure well? Fit Do your goals match the role and the company? Notice what is missing: they will not ask you to reverse a linked list. They want to know what it is like to work with you. Step 1: Turn your projects into stories “I built a REST API” is a fact. A story is better.
articles.author: Gloud Academy

articles.body: An evidence-led assessment and improvement plan, including static websites on free or low-cost CDN hosting 14 October 2026 Photo 1 — Managing a rural business’s public information. 1. Start with the business outcome A rural business does not need to become a media company to benefit from an effective online presence. A farm shop, repair workshop, guesthouse, local food producer, or craft studio needs potential customers to find accurate information, understand the offer, and take a useful next step. An attractive website has limited value if its opening hours are wrong, directions lead to a locked gate, or nobody answers enquiries. Assessment should therefore begin with the customer journey and the business's ability to fulfil demand. Define one primary outcome for the next ninety days.

articles.title: Why Rust Is a Great Fit for Browser-Based Creative Apps
articles.excerpt: Creative desktop software has been dominated by the same few proprietary suites for two decades, and the alternatives that emerged were mostly Electron shells: huge, memory-hungry, and the same perfor…
articles.body:
Creative desktop software has been dominated by the same few proprietary suites for two decades, and the alternatives that emerged were mostly Electron shells: huge, memory-hungry, and the same performance ceiling underneath. Rust plus WebAssembly is quietly changing that equation, and a new wave of browser-based creative tools shows why.

## Why Rust compiles well to this problem

Image editing, vector rendering, and video processing are all compute-heavy, allocation-sensitive workloads. Rust gives you C-class performance without the memory bugs, and wasm-bindgen makes it straightforward to expose that performance to a browser UI.

articles.body: Every sprint refinement meeting seems to face the same unnecessary friction: "Wait, which planning poker tool are we using today?" "I forgot my password, let me reset it..." "Can you invite me to the organization first?" "Wait, my screen hasn't updated yet—did everyone vote?" After watching our engineering team lose 10-15 minutes of productive discussion every single week just getting everyone into the same voting room, I decided to build SwiftPoker . Our core design principle was simple: Zero friction, sub-100ms real-time sync, and no mandatory logins for voters. Here is a breakdown of how we architected the system using Next.js (App Router) and WebSockets . 1. The Real-Time Problem: WebSockets over HTTP Polling In a live planning session, instant feedback is everything.

articles.body: I spent two weeks deep-diving into the AI strategies of the three largest OTAs in the world: Expedia, Booking Holdings, and Trip.com. I read their earnings calls, tested their products, talked to former employees, and analyzed their technical documentation. Conclusion: it's all theater. Not "they're doing some AI and it's not great." Not "their AI is behind the curve." I mean the AI strategies of these three companies are, at their core, performance art designed to convince investors that they're "AI-first" while the actual products remain fundamentally unchanged. articles.excerpt: Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all.
articles.body: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. "If we look at a supernova today, the star's materials are not spread evenly. Oxygen might predominantly fly in one direction, sulphur in another.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope.
